Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 1–3:

(p-622) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (explanation) of Surah al-'Ankabut

This surah is Meccan, except for its opening section, the ten verses, which are Medinan. They were revealed concerning some of the Muslims in Makkah, and there is disagreement on this.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾ ﴿And We certainly tested those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars.﴾

The discussion of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of the surahs has already preceded. Warsh recited "al-M, ahsiba al-nasu an yutraku" with a fatha on the mim, without a hamza after it, and this is based on easing the hamza and transferring its vowel onto the mim.

This verse was revealed concerning a group of believers who were in Makkah, and the disbelievers of Quraysh were harming them and torturing them for Islam, so their hearts were constricted because of that. It may have been deemed strange that Allah would give the disbelievers power over the believers. Mujahid and others said: this verse was revealed as consolation and as informing that this is the way of Allah, blessed and exalted, with His servants: a test for the believers at that time, so that He would know the truthful and see His reward for them, and would know the liar and see His punishment for him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse, although it was revealed for this cause and concerning this group, its meaning remains in the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and its ruling continues for the rest of time. That is because the trial from Allah, exalted, remains on the frontiers of the Muslims through captivity, the afflictions inflicted by the enemy, and other things. And if every place is considered, there is in it such (trial) through sicknesses and various kinds of tribulations. But what resembles the situation of the believers with Quraysh is what we have mentioned, together with the matter of the enemy at every frontier.

Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir, when he was being tortured for Allah, and his like. Al-Sha'bi said: the cause of the verse is what the believers were obligated to; as for the trial, it is the migration (hijrah), from which they were not left exempt; especially since there befell them because of it that the disbelievers followed them, turned them back and fought them, so whoever was killed was killed and whoever was saved was saved. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning Muslims who were in Makkah and disliked jihad and fighting when it was prescribed upon the Prophet ﷺ.

"Hasiba" means "thought" (zanna), and "an" is governed by "hasiba"; it and the clause after it occupy the place of the two objects of "hasiba." The second "an" is in a position of accusative on the assumption that the preposition has been dropped; its implied form is "bi-an yaqulu" (with their saying), and it is possible to estimate "li-an yaqulu" (for their saying). The meaning differs between the ba' and the lam: with the ba', as you say, "I left Zayd in his state," and with the lam it means "for the sake of," i.e., they thought that their belief was a cause for being left.

By "those before them" (alladhina min qablihim) is meant the believers together with the prophets in ancient times.

The majority recited "fa-layaʿlamanna" with a fatha on the ya' and the second lam, and the meaning of that is: He will make manifest His knowledge and bring into existence what He knew from eternity. That is because His knowledge of this from eternity is pre-eternal, and it is merely an expression for bringing into existence in the state that the pre-eternal knowledge comprised. "Truthfulness" and "lying" remain in their usual sense, i.e., whoever is truthful in his action (p-624) and speech, and whoever lies. A group said: it is only a metaphor, and by the two he meant steadfastness in religion, or wavering in it and in jihad against the enemy, and the like. A parallel to this is the verse of Zuhayr:

A lion in Ba'th hunts men, and when the lion lies against his rivals, he is truthful.

Al-Naqqash said: It has been said that the reference of "sadaqu" (those who were truthful) is to Mihja', the freed slave of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, because he was the first of the believers killed on the day of Badr.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "fa-yuʿlimanna" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the second lam, and this reading admits three meanings: first, that He will inform these truthful and lying ones in the Hereafter of their positions in terms of His reward and punishment, and of their deeds in this world, in the sense that He will make them stand over what had come from them; second, that He will inform the people and the world of these truthful and lying ones, i.e., He will expose and publicize them: these in good, and these in evil, and that is in this world and the Hereafter; third, that this may be from the "sign" (ʿalama), i.e., He sets for each group a sign by which it becomes known. On this meaning, the verse is the subject of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever conceals a secret, Allah will clothe him in its cloak." On every one of these meanings there is in it a promise for the truthful believers and a threat for the disbelievers.

Al-Zuhri recited the first as the majority recite it, and the second as the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

Do those who commit evil deeds think they can outrun Us? Evil is their judgment.

Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, the term of Allah is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. And whoever strives, he strives only for himself. Surely Allah is Free of need from the worlds. As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove from them their evil deeds and surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.

"Am" (أمْ) is equivalent to the alif (أ) in His saying "Did they think" (أحَسِبَ). It is as if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, established both groups. He established the believers in their assumption that they would not be tested, and He established the disbelievers, who do evil deeds by torturing the believers and other things, in their assumption that they would outrun the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, and render Him powerless.

His saying, "those who do evil deeds," although the disbelievers are the first intended by it according to the occasion of revelation (nazilah) about which the discourse is concerned, the wording of the verse includes every sinner and doer of evil among the Muslims and others. His saying, "Evil is their judgment" (ساءَ ما يَحْكُمُونَ), the word "ma" (ما) may mean "that which" (الَّذِي), so it is in the position of nominative case (raf'), and it may be in the position of accusative case (nasb), with the implied meaning: "evil is the judgment they pass." In this verse there is a warning to the disbelievers and a consolation to the believers, which appears in His promise of victory on the Day of Resurrection, and that it is coming, since Allah has set its term and informed of it.

In His saying, "Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah," there is a confirmation, meaning: whoever is upon this truth, let him be certain that it is coming and let him increase in insight. Abu 'Ubayda said: "yarju" (يَرْجُو) here means "yakhafu" (يَخافُ), "fears," but the correct view is that hope (raja') here retains its usual meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is the meeting with the reward of Allah. His saying, "And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," its meaning is: He hears the statements of every group, and He knows the beliefs that they hold.

His saying, "And whoever strives, he strives only for himself," is an announcement that each person is repaid for his good deed, so it is his share, which he should not neglect. Allah is Free of need from his striving and from all the worlds entirely.

These two verses are, as it were, [.....] directed toward the wavering, hesitant group concerning the trial by the disbelievers, who used to deny that the disbelievers could inflict any harm upon the believers, and they doubted because of that. So it is as if it were said to them: whoever believes in the Resurrection, the matter is true in itself, and Allah is ever watchful (bi-l-mirsad), meaning: this is an insight that one should not hold for anyone's sake. Likewise, whoever strives, the fruit of his striving is for himself, so he should not bestow favour upon anyone by it. This is like what a debater says when laying out his argument: "Whoever wishes to look at the truth, the matter is such and such," and similar to this, so reflect upon it.

It has also been said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever strives against his enemy for his own sake, not desiring the face of Allah, his striving is for himself and not for Allah, and it is not for Allah through his striving.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 29, verses 8–11:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you about what you used to do.﴾ ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of Allah. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed, we were with you." Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of the worlds?﴾ ﴿And Allah will surely know those who believed, and He will surely know the hypocrites.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: "We have enjoined..." up to the end of the verse. It is narrated from Qatadah that it was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, (p-627) because he migrated (hajara), and his mother swore that she would not shade herself from the sun until he returned to her and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). He persisted in his migration, and the verse was revealed. It is also said that it was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, because something similar happened to him regarding his religion, when Abu Jahl, may the curse of Allah be upon him, deceived him and returned him to his mother... the hadith is in the books of the Prophet's biography (sirah). There is no doubt that it was revealed concerning those among the believers in Makkah who were distressed by the striving of their parents regarding the matter of Islam and the emigration (hijrah). The purpose of this verse appears to be the prohibition of obeying the two parents in such a grave matter. Since the dutifulness to parents and obeying them is among the matters that the Shari'ah has established and affirmed, and it is among the strongly binding obligations in their eyes, the Exalted placed before the prohibition of obeying them in associating partners with Allah His saying: ﴿We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents,﴾ meaning: We do not permit the disobedience of parents, but we do not give them authority over obedience to Allah the Exalted, especially in matters of faith and disbelief.

His saying "kindness" (husnan) may be read as an object (maf'ul), and in that there is a figurative usage (tajawwuz). What makes this easier is that it is general in meaning, as you say: "I enjoined you good," or "I enjoined you evil," by which you express the whole of what you said to him. What strengthens this without a preposition is that the preposition appears in His saying "to his parents," since the meaning is: "We enjoined man to act with goodness toward his parents." A parallel to this is the words of the poet:

"I am amazed at Dahma'a when she complains of us, and at the father of Dahma'a when he enjoins us: 'Good to her,' as though we had been harsh to her."

It is also possible that the second object is "to his parents," and "kindness" (husnan) is in the accusative by a hidden verb whose estimate is: "he shows kindness, a kindness," and it is in the accusative in the manner of a verbal noun (masdar). 'Isa and al-Jahdari read "hasanan" with two fathas. Al-Jahdari said: "In the Imam (the standard codex) it is written: 'to his parents, ihsanan (kindness).'" Abu Hatim said: "He means it is like in al-Ahqaf." Al-Tha'labi said: "In the Mushaf (copy) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it is: 'ihsanan.'" His saying the Exalted: ﴿To Me is your return﴾ is a warning regarding obeying the parents in matters of disbelief.

Then the Exalted repeated the illustration of the state of the believers in order to move souls to attain their ranks. His saying the Exalted: ﴿We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾ is an intensification, meaning: those who are at the utmost of righteousness and its farthest ends. When this ruling is attained by the believers, its fruit is attained, and its reward is Paradise.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And among the people﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And He will surely know the hypocrites﴾ was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who were in Makkah, concealing their Islam. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "When the disbelievers of Quraysh went out to Badr, they took with them a group of these people, and some of them were struck down. The Muslims said: 'They were our companions, and they were compelled,' and they asked forgiveness for them. Then this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 97], the verse." He said: "The Muslims then wrote to those who remained in Makkah with this verse, and that there was no excuse for them. So they went out, and the polytheists overtook them, subjected them to trial, and returned them to Makkah. Then the verse was revealed about them: ﴿And among the people is he who says, 'We believe in Allah'﴾ the verse. The Muslims wrote to them with that, and they grieved and despaired of every good. Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then fought and were patient—indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. The Muslims wrote to them with that, and that Allah the Exalted had made for them a way out. So they went out, and the polytheists overtook them (p-629) and fought them. Some escaped, and some were killed."

Ibn Zayd said: His saying the Exalted: ﴿made the trial of people﴾ was revealed concerning hypocrites who disbelieved when they were harmed.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿the trial of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ means: the harm of people was difficult for him when they hindered him. His duty was not to pay attention to it, and to be patient with it in return for his salvation from the punishment of Allah the Exalted. Then the Exalted removed the basis of their reliance and their deception, with His saying: "if victory comes." Then He established them upon the knowledge of Allah the Exalted regarding what is in their breasts. That is: had they possessed complete certainty and sincere Islam, they would not have hesitated for a moment, and they would have faced every terror in order to emigrate and reach the abode of their Prophet.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah will surely know those who believed, and He will surely know the hypocrites﴾, its explanation is according to the same principle as what preceded regarding its counterpart.

Here the Madani (Medinan) part of this surah ends.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 18–20:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And if you deny, then [many] communities before you have denied. And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾ ﴿Have they not considered how Allah originates creation and then repeats it? Concerning His saying, ﴿And if you deny﴾ — the verse is a warning: that is, others before you have denied and were punished. The Messenger's duty is only conveyance, and after that every person is held accountable for his deeds.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim (according to one of the two transmissions from him) read "أو لَمْ تَرَوْا" (awa lam tarawā, with the ta', "have you not seen"), while the rest read "أو لَمْ يَرَوْا" (awa lam yarawā, with the ya', "have they not seen"). The first is addressed in the second person, and the second is a report about the absent party. The majority read "يُبْدِئُ" (yubdi'u, "originates"), while al-Zubayr, 'Isa and Abu 'Amr (according to one of the two transmissions from him) read "يَبْدَأُ" (yabda'u, "begins").

These references are to what appears with the reporting of the revival of the earth and plants, their return, and the like, which are evidence of resurrection from the graves and gathering. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Have they not seen, by means of proofs and reflection, how it is possible for Allah, blessed and exalted, to restore bodies after death?" This is the interpretation of Qatadah. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the meaning is, how He originates the creation of man and then returns him to other states, until [he returns] to dust. Muqatil said: "creation" in this verse refers to the night and the day.

Then Allah, exalted, commanded His Prophet — and it is possible that this refers to Muhammad, if it is in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, it is an interjection between two statements — to command them, by way of argument, to travel through the earth and to observe every region and every nation, past and present, for indeed this shows that there is no creator except Allah, blessed and exalted, and no one who originates creation besides Him. Then He related, by way of information, that Allah, exalted, is the one who initiates the production of the resurrection from the graves.

(p-635) Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "النَشاءَةُ" (al-nasha'ah) on the pattern of (al-fa'alah), and this is the reading of al-A'raj, just as one says "ra'fah" and "ra'afah" (both meaning compassion). The rest read "النَشْأةَ" (al-nash'ah) on the pattern of (al-fa'lah). al-Zuhri read "النَشَّةَ" (al-nashshah) with a doubled shin throughout the Qur'an. As for the resurrection from the graves, the evidence of reason establishes its possibility, and the revealed laws have informed of its occurrence and existence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verse 21–23:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills, and to Him you will be turned back.﴾ ﴿And you cannot escape [Him] in the earth or in the heaven, and you have no protector or helper besides Allah.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and in His meeting, it is they who have despaired of My mercy, and it is they for whom there is a painful punishment.﴾

The meaning: He facilitates for whomever He wills the deeds of those upon whom punishment is due, and He facilitates for whomever He wills the deeds of those for whom happiness has preceded. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 24–25:**

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of Allah as a bond of affection among you in the worldly life; then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and curse one another, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited "jawaba" (answer) in the accusative (naṣb), while al-Hasan recited "jawabu" in the nominative (raf'), and likewise Salim al-Aftas. Allah, exalted is He, informs us that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, set out the proofs and clarified the matter of the religion, they resorted to domination and abandoned the way of argument, though they had not previously had any recourse to it. So they conspired to kill him and to burn him with fire, and they carried out the order to burn him as has been explained at length in other places. Allah, exalted is He, saved him from their fire and made it "coolness and safety" (bardan wa salaman) for him. Ka'b al-Ahbar (may God have mercy on him) said: "The fire burned only the bonds with which they had tied him. Allah made this a sign and a lesson, and a proof of His oneness for whomever He expands the breast and facilitates for faith." That is: this category of people benefits from the sign, while for the disbelievers it is blindness, even though in itself it is a sign for all.

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentions that Ibrahim made them acknowledge that their taking of idols and images was only a matter of some of them following others, and a preservation of their worldly affections and loves; and that on the Day of Resurrection some of them will deny others and curse one another, because their mutual affection was not based on piety. And [compare] ﴿Friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

Ibn 'Amir, Nafi', 'Asim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr), and Abu 'Amr (in the transmission of Abu Zayd) recited "mawaddata baynikum" with tanwin and the accusative (naṣb) on both "mawaddata" and "bayna". 'Asim (in the transmission of al-A'mash from Abu Bakr) recited "mawaddatun" in the nominative and "baynikum" in the genitive (khafḍ). The justification for the reading with the nominative "mawaddatun" is that "ma" may be a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi" (that which). In the phrase "ittakhadhtum" there is a pronoun referring to "alladhi"; this pronoun is the first object of "ittakhadhtum", "awthanan" (idols) is the second object, and "mawaddatun" is the predicate of "inna" according to the reading of one who gives it tanwin, and likewise according to the reading of one who does not give it tanwin. It is also possible that "ma" is a "kafṣa" (a particle that neutralizes the governing power of "inna", i.e. "inna" becomes "innama"), in which case there is no pronoun in "ittakhadhtum", and "awthanan" is the object of "ittakhadhtum" which is then restricted to it; one supplies a second object such as "alihatan" (gods) or similar, just as one supplies it in Allah's words ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ [al-A'raf: 152], meaning "a god". Then "mawaddatun" is the predicate of an inchoative (mubtada') whose implied form is "huwa mawaddatun" (it is a bond of affection). In these interpretations there is metaphor and extension in calling the idols "mawaddah", or else there is an elided genitive construction (ḥadhf muḍāf) [i.e., "mawaddata" stands for "dhū mawaddah" or "sabab mawaddah"].

As for the one who recited "mawaddata" in the accusative, the reading is based on "ma" being a "kafṣa", and on "ittakhadhtum" being free of a pronoun, with restriction to the single object as already explained. "Al-mawaddata" is then the object for which (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., an accusative of purpose.

Whoever made "mawaddata" a genitive construct (idafa) to "al-bayn" in both readings, the accusative and the nominative, has permitted this, and has treated the adverbial noun (zarf) as functioning like nouns. Whoever recited "baynakum" in the accusative in both readings, the accusative and the nominative for "mawaddata", it is likewise possible that it is put in the accusative as an adverb (zarf), and it is then linked to "mawaddata". Likewise ﴿And he said, "You have taken"﴾ is also an adverb linked to "mawaddata". It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has operated on two adverbs, in that time and place differ; had both been of one kind it would not be permissible, as you say, "I saw Zayd yesterday in the market," and you do not say, "I saw Zayd yesterday last night," except where one of the two adverbs is part of the other, as you say, "I saw Zayd yesterday in the evening." It is also permissible for "baynakum" to be in the accusative as an attribute (sifa) of "mawaddah", and here there is an elided and implied element, its implied form being "mawaddatan thabitatan baynakum" (a firm affection between you). In the adverb there is a pronoun referring to "mawaddah"; when "thabitatan" is elided, the pronoun settles into the adverb itself. And the phrase ﴿And he said, "You have taken"﴾ is an adverbial clause in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun present in "baynikum" after the elision of "thabitatin". This state is linked to "mawaddah", and its linking to it is permissible even though it has been described, because the meaning of the verb is within it; and although it has been described, it is not prohibited that the meaning of the verb should operate, except on the object. But in the adverb and in the state it does operate. Makki said: It is also permissible that "fi al-hayah" (in the life) be a fixed attribute of "mawaddah", and that in it there is an implied "musta'iratan" (established/settled), and in it there is a second pronoun referring back to "mawaddah". The meaning, on this basis, is: the affection among you is settled in the worldly life.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

It is also valid that "mawaddah" in the reading of one who recited it in the accusative be a second object of "ittakhadhtum", and this involves extension, so reflect on it. In the codex of Ubayy it reads "mawaddata baynihim" with a ha' (his/their), and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "innama mawaddatu baynikum".

Allah, exalted is He, informs us that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, set out the proofs and clarified the matter of the religion, they resorted to domination and abandoned the way of argument, though they had not previously had any recourse to it. So they conspired to kill him and to burn him with fire, and they carried out the order to burn him as has been explained at length in other places. Allah, exalted is He, saved him from their fire and made it "coolness and safety" (bardan wa salaman) for him. Ka'b al-Ahbar (may God have mercy on him) said: "The fire burned only the bonds with which they had tied him. Allah made this a sign and a lesson, and a proof of His oneness for whomever He expands the breast and facilitates for faith." That is: this category of people benefits from the sign, while for the disbelievers it is blindness, even though in itself it is a sign for all.

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentions that Ibrahim made them acknowledge that their taking of idols and images was only a matter of some of them following others, and a preservation of their worldly affections and loves; and that on the Day of Resurrection some of them will deny others and curse one another, because their mutual affection was not based on piety. And [compare] ﴿Friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

Ibn 'Amir, Nafi', 'Asim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr), and Abu 'Amr (in the transmission of Abu Zayd) recited "mawaddata baynikum" with tanwin and the accusative (naṣb) on both "mawaddata" and "bayna". 'Asim (in the transmission of al-A'mash from Abu Bakr) recited "mawaddatun" in the nominative and "baynikum" in the genitive (khafḍ). The justification for the reading with the nominative "mawaddatun" is that "ma" may be a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi" (that which). In the phrase "ittakhadhtum" there is a pronoun referring to "alladhi"; this pronoun is the first object of "ittakhadhtum", "awthanan" (idols) is the second object, and "mawaddatun" is the predicate of "inna" according to the reading of one who gives it tanwin, and likewise according to the reading of one who does not give it tanwin. It is also possible that "ma" is a "kafṣa" (a particle that neutralizes the governing power of "inna", i.e. "inna" becomes "innama"), in which case there is no pronoun in "ittakhadhtum", and "awthanan" is the object of "ittakhadhtum" which is then restricted to it; one supplies a second object such as "alihatan" (gods) or similar, just as one supplies it in Allah's words ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ [al-A'raf: 152], meaning "a god". Then "mawaddatun" is the predicate of an inchoative (mubtada') whose implied form is "huwa mawaddatun" (it is a bond of affection). In these interpretations there is metaphor and extension in calling the idols "mawaddah", or else there is an elided genitive construction (ḥadhf muḍāf) [i.e., "mawaddata" stands for "dhū mawaddah" or "sabab mawaddah"].

As for the one who recited "mawaddata" in the accusative, the reading is based on "ma" being a "kafṣa", and on "ittakhadhtum" being free of a pronoun, with restriction to the single object as already explained. "Al-mawaddata" is then the object for which (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., an accusative of purpose.

Whoever made "mawaddata" a genitive construct (idafa) to "al-bayn" in both readings, the accusative and the nominative, has permitted this, and has treated the adverbial noun (zarf) as functioning like nouns. Whoever recited "baynakum" in the accusative in both readings, the accusative and the nominative for "mawaddata", it is likewise possible that it is put in the accusative as an adverb (zarf), and it is then linked to "mawaddata". Likewise ﴿And he said, "You have taken"﴾ is also an adverb linked to "mawaddata". It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has operated on two adverbs, in that time and place differ; had both been of one kind it would not be permissible, as you say, "I saw Zayd yesterday in the market," and you do not say, "I saw Zayd yesterday last night," except where one of the two adverbs is part of the other, as you say, "I saw Zayd yesterday in the evening." It is also permissible for "baynakum" to be in the accusative as an attribute (sifa) of "mawaddah", and here there is an elided and implied element, its implied form being "mawaddatan thabitatan baynakum" (a firm affection between you). In the adverb there is a pronoun referring to "mawaddah"; when "thabitatan" is elided, the pronoun settles into the adverb itself. And the phrase ﴿And he said, "You have taken"﴾ is an adverbial clause in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun present in "baynikum" after the elision of "thabitatin". This state is linked to "mawaddah", and its linking to it is permissible even though it has been described, because the meaning of the verb is within it; and although it has been described, it is not prohibited that the meaning of the verb should operate, except on the object. But in the adverb and in the state it does operate. Makki said: It is also permissible that "fi al-hayah" (in the life) be a fixed attribute of "mawaddah", and that in it there is an implied "musta'iratan" (established/settled), and in it there is a second pronoun referring back to "mawaddah". The meaning, on this basis, is: the affection among you is settled in the worldly life.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

It is also valid that "mawaddah" in the reading of one who recited it in the accusative be a second object of "ittakhadhtum", and this involves extension, so reflect on it. In the codex of Ubayy it reads "mawaddata baynihim" with a ha' (his/their), and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "innama mawaddatu baynikum".

"Qawluhu 'azza wa jall":

﴿So Lot believed him. And he said, "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed, He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And [mention] Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed, you commit an abomination that no one among the worlds has preceded you in."﴾

"Amana" (believed) means "saddaqa" (affirmed as true), and it is a verb that takes the prepositions "bi" and "li." The one who said ﴿Indeed, I am emigrating﴾ is Abraham, peace be upon him, as related by Qatada and al-Nakha'i. A group said it was Lot, peace be upon him.

Among the narrations that are authentic is that Abraham and Lot emigrated from their town of "Kuthā," which is in the countryside of Kufa, in the land of Babylon, to the lands of the Levant, Palestine and elsewhere. Ibn Jurayj said: they emigrated to Harran, and then they were afterwards commanded to go to the Levant. During this emigration Sarah was in the company of Abraham, and the matter of the king befell her.

"Al-muhajir" (the emigrant): the one who departs from a matter. In the usage of the Sharia, it is the one who leaves his homeland seeking the pleasure of Allah, Exalted. The Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) took this name before the Conquest. His saying ﴿the Almighty, the Wise﴾ together with the emigration "to Him" are two eloquent attributes that necessitate the deserving of reliance upon Him. In His saying ﴿to my Lord﴾ there is an elision of a noun, its implied meaning being: "to the pleasure of my Lord," or something similar.

Isaac, son of Abraham, is the one whose good news was given to him, and the good news of Jacob came after him; he is the son of Isaac. "Al-kitab" (the Book) is a noun of genus: that is, Allah, Exalted, placed in the descendants of Abraham, peace be upon him, all the revealed Books: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Furqan, and Jesus, peace be upon him, is among his descendants. His saying ﴿his reward in this world﴾ means: during his lifetime, such that he witnessed that and was gladdened by it. The reward that Allah, Exalted, gave him was well-being from the Fire, from the unjust king, good deeds, and a good reputation. This was said by Mujahid. And that every nation takes him as its guide; this was said by Ibn Jurayj. And the child in whom the eye is comforted, in accordance with obedience to Allah, Exalted; this was said by al-Hasan. Then He informed concerning him that in the Hereafter he is among the ranks of the righteous who attained the pleasure of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and triumphed with His mercy and His supreme honor.

His saying, Exalted: "Lot" is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, its implied meaning being: "And mention Lot." And "al-fahisha" (the abomination): (p-640) the practice of men with men in the anus, and it is a disobedience that the people of Lot invented.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 29–31:

The Exalted said:

﴿Do you really commit lewdness, and cut off the road, and commit the foul deed in your gatherings?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good tidings, they said, "We are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers."﴾

The variant readings (qira'at, recitations) of "A-innakum" have already been mentioned. People differed regarding "qat' al-sabil" (cutting off the road) referred to here. One group said: the cutting of the road was by robbery, which was widespread among them. Ibn Zayd said: they would block the roads for people in order to pursue indecency, so they would commit injustice (yahifun). Another group said: rather, it meant cutting off the path of procreation by abandoning women and having intercourse with men. Another group said: it meant that by spreading gossip about people they would cut off people's path from their intended dealings in trade and other matters. "Al-nadi" is the assembly in which people gather; it is a generic noun, since the assemblies in cities are many, as if he said: "and you commit it in your gatherings wherever you gather." People differed regarding "al-munkar" (the evil deed). One group said: they would pelt people with pebbles and make light of strangers and passersby, and Umm Hani narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). They were not restrained by religion or manliness. Mujahid and Mansur said: they would have intercourse with men in their assemblies while some of them watched others. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: their evil was that they would engage in sexual acts with one another in their gatherings; this was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: they would break wind (yatadarratun) in their gatherings. Mujahid also said: their practice was pigeon-flying, dyeing the fingertips with henna, whistling, pelting pebbles, and abandoning modesty in all their affairs. (p. 641)

Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

These things may be found among some sinners of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), so forbidding them is obligatory.

When Lut (peace be upon him) confronted them with these abominations, they returned to denial and obstinacy, meaning: "Bring us the punishment," for that will not happen, and you have no power over it. They only said this while being resolved upon the belief that he was lying, and it is not sound by natural disposition for a stubborn person to say this. [Then Lut (peace be upon him) sought help from his Lord, so He sent angels to punish them.] They came first to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) bringing good news of Ishaq and good news of Lut's victory over his people. Their meeting with Ibrahim took the form described in other places. Thus the word "al-bushra" (the good tidings) in this context includes the matter of Ishaq and the support of Lut, peace be upon them both. When they informed him of the destruction of the town for its wrongdoing, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) felt compassion for Lut (peace be upon him), so he argued with them according to what follows.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 32–35:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said, "Indeed, in it is Lut." They said, "We are most knowing of who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is of those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed by them and felt powerless to protect them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is of those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿Indeed, we will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky because they have been defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason.﴾

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, learned from the angels that the town of Lut was going to be punished, he felt compassion for the believers, so he argued with the angels and said, "Do you see? If there are a hundred houses of believers in it, will you still destroy them?" They said, "There are no such believers in it." He kept lowering the number until he reached ten houses. The angels said to him, "There are not ten in it, nor five, nor three, nor two." At that point Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said, "Indeed, in it is Lut." So they replied to him, "We are most knowing of who is in it," meaning: do not fear that any harm will befall a believer.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ" (la-nunajjiyannahu) with a fatha on the middle nun and a shadda on the jim, and "مُنَجُّوكَ" (munajjuka) with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the jim. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "لَنُنْجِيَنَّهُ" (la-nunjiyannahu) with a sukun on the nun and a light jim. Ibn Kathir and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ" with the shadda, and "مُنْجُوكَ" (munjuka) with no shadda. A group read "لَنُنْجِيَنْهُ" with a sukun on the final nun of the word. This reading is only possible on the basis that they lightened the doubled nun while still intending it.

The wife of Lut here was an unbeliever, and she would alert the enemies to his guests. "Al-ghabir" (the remaining) means the one who stays behind. Its meaning is: among those who remain behind in punishment. A group said: "of those who remain behind" means among those who lingered and stayed behind among the people, and persisted in their disbelief. The pronoun in "بِهِمْ" (bihim) in both places refers to the guests, the messengers, and the distress was due to his fear for them from his people. When they informed him of their situation, he was relieved. The majority of reciters read "سِيءَ" (si'a) with a kasra on the sin. 'Isa and Talha read it with a damma. "Al-rijz" (the punishment) means torment. His saying, exalted is He, "بِما كانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ" (bima kanu yafsuqun), means: their punishment is because of their wickedness. Likewise, every nation that Allah punished, He punished only for wickedness and disobedience, but such wickedness is coupled with disbelief, which necessitates the punishment of the Hereafter. The words of the Most High:

And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿And these parables We present to people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable.﴾

Glorious and exalted is He, has likened the disbelievers in their worship of idols, and in their building all their affairs upon that, to the spider, which builds and exerts effort, yet all of its affairs are weak: whenever even a slight breeze (هابَّة, hābba) touches it, it is overwhelmed. Likewise, the state of those people and their striving is collapsing, having no strength and no support. And from a report mentioned by al-Naqqash (al-Naqqash, a transmitter and exegete): "The spider is a devil whom Allah transformed, so kill it." It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Clean your houses of spider webs, for leaving them brings poverty." As for the words of the Most High, ﴿if only they knew﴾, the meaning is: if only they knew that this is their parable, and that their state and their connection to the truth is this condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 44–45:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth. Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾ ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing. And the remembrance of Allah is greater. And Allah knows what you do.﴾

In mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth, He draws attention to a matter whereby the mind perceives the smallness of the worth of idols and of every object of worship besides Allah, the Exalted. His saying, Glorified is He, "with truth," means: with what is necessary and luminous, not in vain or for play, but so that it may indicate His authority, establish His laws, set forth proofs for their people, and spread benefits, along with other things that cannot be counted.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to submit to His command, to recite the Qur'an that was revealed to him, and to establish the prayer, meaning to maintain it constantly and to uphold its limits. Then He informed, as a judgment from Him, that the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My view on this is that when the worshipper is upon what is required of humility, submissiveness, remembrance of Allah the Exalted, and imagining standing before Him, and that his heart and sincerity are being observed and watched, his soul becomes disposed to that and humbled, and the awareness of Allah, blessed and exalted, pervades it. Thus it persists in that in its words and deeds, and it refrains from immorality and wrongdoing. It hardly ceases from this until another prayer overshadows him, by which he returns to the best state. This is the meaning of this statement, for the prayer of a believer should be like this. It is related from some of the early generation (salaf) that whenever he stood for prayer he would tremble and his color would turn pale. He was asked about this and said: "I am standing before Allah, blessed and exalted, and it is right for me to feel this even before the kings of this world; so how much more before the King of kings?"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So this is a prayer that necessarily forbids immorality and wrongdoing. As for one whose prayer revolves around merely fulfilling the obligation, with no humility, no remembrance, and no virtues, such a person leaves his station wherever he is. If he is on a path of sins that distance him from Allah the Exalted, he continues in his distance. On this basis the report from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and al-A'mash is explained, namely their saying: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from immorality and wrongdoing increases in nothing but distance from Allah." It has been related that al-Hasan transmitted it from the Prophet ﷺ, but that is not sound in its chain. I heard Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, say: When we consider its wording and examine its meaning, it is not permissible to say that the very prayer of the disobedient person distances him from Allah, the Exalted, to the point that it is like a sin. Rather, it is to be understood as meaning that it does not affect bringing him closer to Allah the Exalted; it leaves him in his state and his sins of immorality and wrongdoing and distance, so the prayer adds nothing but confirmation of that distance which was his path. It is as though it distanced him when it did not restrain his distance from Allah the Exalted. It was said to Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "So-and-so prays a great deal." He said: "It benefits only the one who obeys it."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas recited: "Indeed the prayer enjoins what is good and forbids immorality and wrongdoing." Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The prayer here is the Qur'an." Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Kalbi said: "Indeed the prayer forbids (evil) for as long as you are in it."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a non-Arabic (or weak) interpretation. How does this compare with what Anas ibn Malik related? He said: "There was a young man from the Ansar who prayed with the Prophet ﷺ but did not leave any immorality or theft without committing it. This was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'His prayer will restrain him.' He did not wait long before he repented and his condition became good. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Did I not tell you?'"

As for His saying, ﴿and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Darda', Salman, Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Qurra, may Allah be pleased with all the Companions, said: its meaning is: the remembrance of Allah of you is greater than your remembrance of Him. It was also said: its meaning is: the remembrance of Allah is greater together with persistence in prayer in forbidding immorality and wrongdoing. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the remembrance of Allah is greater than everything. It was said to Salman: "Which deeds are best?" He said: "Do you not read the Qur'an: ﴿and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾?" He seems to encourage it in these last two interpretations.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, the meaning is: the remembrance of Allah is greater in absolute terms, that is, it is what forbids immorality and wrongdoing. The part of it that is in the prayer does this, and it does so likewise outside the prayer, because refraining is only done by one who remembers and is mindful of Him. The reward of that remembrance is that Allah the Exalted remembers him, as in the hadith: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than theirs." The movements of the prayer have no effect in forbidding, and beneficial remembrance is that which is with knowledge, the heart's attentiveness, and its being free of anything other than Allah the Exalted. As for what does not go beyond the tongue, it is in a different rank. Allah's remembrance of the servant is the outpouring of guidance and the light of knowledge upon him, and that is the fruit of the servant's remembrance of his Lord. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152]. The rest of the verse is a form of warning and exhortation toward mindfulness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verse 46:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best, except for those of them who have wronged. And say, "We believe in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to you. And our God and your God is one, and we are Muslims [in submission] to Him."﴾

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "illa" (except) as an exception particle. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, read "alla" with a fatha on the hamza and a light lam, and the exegetes differed concerning the intended meaning of this verse.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: do not argue with those among the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). It is as if he said, "The People of the Book who are believers." ﴿except in a way that is best﴾, meaning by agreement concerning what they relate to you of the reports of their predecessors and other things. His saying, Exalted is He, according to this interpretation, ﴿except those who have wronged﴾, he means by it those of them who remained upon their disbelief, such as those who disbelieved and betrayed among the Banu Qurayza, the Nadir and others. So the verse, according to this, is muhkam (definitive), not abrogated.

Mujahid said: what is meant by the People of the Book is the Jews and the Christians who remain upon their religion. Allah, Exalted is He, commanded the believers not to argue with them except in the best manner: by calling to Allah, Exalted is He, and drawing attention to His signs, in hope of their responding to faith, not by way of harshness and roughness. His saying, according to this interpretation, ﴿except those of them who have wronged﴾ means: those who wronged you. Otherwise, all of them are wrongdoers absolutely. The verse, according to this, is abrogated concerning the truce with those who do not fight. Qatada said: it is abrogated by the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 29], the verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to be the correct meaning of the verse becomes clear only by knowing the circumstances at the time the verse was revealed. That is because the surah is Meccan after the first ten verses, and at that time there was no obligatory fighting, nor any demand for jizya, nor anything else of that sort. The Jews were in Mecca and in its surroundings, so there may have occurred between them and the believers argument, contention and disputation in matters of religion, and denial. So Allah, Exalted is He, commanded the believers not to argue with them through disputation except in the best manner, which is calling to Allah, Exalted is He, and gentleness. Then He excepted those among them who wronged the believers, either by an action, or by a statement, or by harming Muhammad (ﷺ), or by openly declaring a gross disbelief, such as the saying of some of them: "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the like. For this attribute was excepted, meaning that it was permissible for the People of Islam to oppose it by going beyond the manner that is best. Then this was afterwards abrogated by the verse of fighting and jizya. This is the saying of Qatada.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And say, "We believe"﴾, the verse. Abu Hurayra said: The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and would interpret it in Arabic for the Muslims. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not believe the People of the Book, nor deny them, but say: ﴿We believe in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to you, and our God and your God is one, and we are Muslims [in submission] to Him.﴾"

And Abdullah ibn Mas'ud narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not ask the People of the Book about anything, for they will not guide you while they have gone astray. Either you will deny a truth, or you will affirm a falsehood."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verse 47–49:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿And thus have We sent down to you the Book. Those to whom We have given the Book believe in it, and among these there are those who believe in it. And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; for then would the falsifiers have doubted.﴾ ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge. The discussion preceding this verse included what implies the sending down of a law and a Book from God upon prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore, the conjunction of "And thus have We sent down to you the Book" is appropriately linked to what is implicit in the context, meaning: "And as We sent down to those before you, We have sent down to you the Book." And "the Book" means the Qur'an.

Then He informed about the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) that among them also are those who believe in it, though they had not yet believed; in this report there is a declaration of the unseen, which its occurrence afterward manifested. Then He condemned those who deny from a community whose predecessors had believed in the past and some of whom believed in the recent times, and those among them who deny have attained the highest rank of misguidance. It is also likely that the disbelievers of Quraysh are intended in this condemnation together with the disbelievers of the Children of Israel.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and the saying of al-Baji, may Allah have mercy on him, is among it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 50–52:**

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿And they say, "Why were no signs sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them? Indeed, in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth. And those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah—those are the losers."﴾

The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the Quraysh and some of the Jews, because they used to teach the Quraysh this same argument: "Has there not come to you the like of what Moses brought, such as the staff and others?" Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and 'Ali ibn Nasr on the authority of Abu 'Amr read "āyatun min rabbihi" (a single sign). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read "āyātun" (signs). Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet ﷺ to teach them that this matter is in the hand of Allah, blessed and exalted, and that it is not brought down by suggestion and wishing, and that He sent him only as a warner and was not commanded to do anything other than that. In the codex of Ubayy: "Lawla ma ya'tinā bi-āyātin min rabbihi, qul innamā al-āyātu" (Why does he not bring us signs from his Lord? Say, the signs are only...).

Then He argued against them in their demand for a sign by the matter of the Qur'an, which is the greatest of signs and a miracle for both jinn and humankind, so He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book﴾. Then He affirmed what it contains of mercy and reminder for the believers. Thus His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾ is an answer to the one who said ﴿Why was it not sent down﴾.

Al-Tabari related that this verse was revealed because of "a group of believers who came to the Prophet ﷺ with books in which they had written some of what the Jews were saying, those who had informed them of something from the Torah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ rejected that and said: 'Is this not sufficient as misguidance for a people who turned away from what their Prophet brought them to what someone else brought.'" And the verse was revealed concerning that.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first interpretation fits better with the sequence of the verses.

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet ﷺ to rely on the command of Allah, blessed and exalted, and to make Him his sufficiency as a witness and judge between him and them, with His knowledge and His comprehension of all their affairs. His saying "bil-batil" (in falsehood) means: with the idols and images and what follows their matter of beliefs. Falsehood is when an act is done that is intended to achieve some matter, while that matter does not come about from that act. The idols were believed by their worshippers to bring about the most perfect and most successful outcome, but the most perfect and most correct course is only to abandon them. So they are falsehood. The rest of the verse is clear.

O My servants who have believed, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone. Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: His words, "Indeed My earth is vast," are a promise of the breadth of provision throughout the whole earth.

Likewise Nafi' and 'Asim recited "ardi" with a sukun. His words, "fa-iyaya" (so Me alone), are in the accusative governed by a verb understood from the context, its estimated form being "fa-iyaya u'buduu fa'budun" ("so worship Me alone, so worship Me"), for emphasis also in the estimation.

His words, "Every soul will taste death," the verse, are a belittling of the affairs of this world and its fears, as if some of the believers considered what would befall them upon leaving their homeland, that they might die or go hungry and the like. His words, "ghurafan," is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, the estimate being "in chambers." Ya'qub recited "lanubawwiyannahum" with a ya' below, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Amir: "ghurafan" with a damma on the ghayn and the ra'.

Then He described them with patience and reliance upon Allah, and these two comprise all goodness, meaning: patience in obedience and patience against desires.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 60–63:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they turned away?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky, and gives life thereby to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾

"Ka'ayyin" means "kam" (how many). This verse is an exhortation to emigration (hijrah), because some of the believers reflected on the poverty and hunger that would befall them in emigration, and they said: "Estrangement in a land where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them the example of most of the animals, which seek their sustenance, do not store, and do not worry about their provision. The meaning is: He provides for you, so prefer obedience to Allah the Exalted above everything else. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿does not carry﴾ may mean: from carrying, i.e., it does not transport and does not look to store it; this was said by Ibn Mijlaz, Mujahid, and 'Ali ibn al-Aqmar.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Storing is not the trait of those who have certainty (yaqin), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "How will you be when you remain among a worthless remnant of people who hoard a year's provision out of weakness of certainty?" It is also possible that it means from "carrying" in the sense of bearing a burden, i.e., it does not take upon itself its provision and does not worry about it.

Then Allah the Exalted addressed His Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the disbelievers and establishing the proof against them: that if they were asked about the great matters which are signs of power, they would have no option but to concede that they belong to Allah the Exalted. "Yu'fakun" means: they are turned away. Blessed and Exalted is He, drew attention to the creation of the heavens and the earth, the subjugation of the stars, and the mention of their greatness (p-659), and He drew attention to the extension and restriction of provision for a people, and the sending down of rain from the sky. These are many lessons for whoever reflects, toward salvation and the most upright belief. Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to praise Him, in a manner rebuking their intellects, and He judged concerning them that most of them do not reason, and no sign of reflection appears from them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 60–63:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they turned away?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky, and gives life thereby to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾

"Ka'ayyin" means "kam" (how many). This verse is an exhortation to emigration (hijrah), because some of the believers reflected on the poverty and hunger that would befall them in emigration, and they said: "Estrangement in a land where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them the example of most of the animals, which seek their sustenance, do not store, and do not worry about their provision. The meaning is: He provides for you, so prefer obedience to Allah the Exalted above everything else. The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Storing is not the trait of those who have certainty (yaqin), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "How will you be when you remain among a worthless remnant of people who hoard a year's provision out of weakness of certainty?" "Yu'fakun" means: they are turned away. Blessed and Exalted is He, drew attention to the creation of the heavens and the earth, the subjugation of the stars, and the mention of their greatness (p-659), and He drew attention to the extension and restriction of provision for a people, and the sending down of rain from the sky. These are many lessons for whoever reflects, toward salvation and the most upright belief. Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to praise Him, in a manner rebuking their intellects, and He judged concerning them that most of them do not reason, and no sign of reflection appears from them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-'Ankabut (29), verses 64–67:**

The words of the Most High:

﴿Surely this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play; and indeed the Abode of the Hereafter, that is the Life, if they only knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincerely devoted to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to the land, behold, they associate partners with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves. But they will soon come to know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away all around them? Will they then believe in falsehood and deny the blessing of Allah?﴾

In this verse, Allah the Most High describes the worldly life as amusement and play, meaning that whatever in it is not for the sake of Allah the Most High. Whatever is for the sake of Allah the Most High belongs to the Hereafter. As for the affairs of this world that exceed the necessities (al-daruri, the essentials) on which the sustenance of life and the strength for acts of obedience depend, they are indeed amusement and play. Reflect on this in clothing, food, drink, speech, and other things.

Consider also that the need of the rich and the poor for essential matters is one and the same: such as breathing air, satisfying hunger, covering the private parts, and protecting oneself from heat and cold. All of these are the greatest matters of living.

The word "al-hayawan" (the Life) and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning. According to Sibawayh and al-Khalil, it is a verbal noun (masdar) like "al-hayaman" and the like. The meaning is: there is no death in it. This is what Mujahid said, and it is a good interpretation. Its original form is "hayayan," and one of the two yas was changed to a waw because two similar letters came together.

Then Allah the Most High made them face their condition at sea during great fear, for every human being forgets every idol and other things, and clings to supplication and turning to Allah, blessed and exalted is He. The words of the Most High, "behold, they associate partners," mean that they return to mentioning their idols and exalting them. His words "so that they may deny" are in the accusative by the lam of purpose (lam kay, the lam expressing purpose). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "wa-liyatamatta'u" with a kasra on the lam. Ibn Kathir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-litatamatta'u" with a sukun on the lam, in the form of a command which is for threat and warning. The waw, according to this reading, joins a clause of speech and not a verb to a verb. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "fa-tamatta'u fa-sawfa ta'lamun," and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "fa-la-sawfa" with a lam.

Then Allah the Most High enumerated for the disbelievers of Quraysh His blessing upon them in the Sanctuary, in that He made it secure for them, free from fear of the conditions and customs of the Arabs and their evil deeds, such as killing and seizing wealth and the like. This is the "takhattuf" (snatching away) in which people were involved. Then He established against them, by way of rebuke, their believing in falsehood and their disbelief in Allah and His blessing. Most reciters read "yu'minun" and "yakfurun" with the ya' (third person). Al-Hasan and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read both with the ta' (second person).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 29, verses 68–69:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. Indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

He, the Mighty and Majestic, established them upon the condition of one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs, and this was their condition. He informed them that there is no one more unjust than him. Within this is a severe warning. Then He clarified the warning further by affirming the matter of Hell. Al-mathwa (المثوى) is the place of residence. The wording of these verses is extremely concise and brief, while comprehensive in meanings.

Then He, may He be exalted, mentioned the condition of His allies and those who strive for Him, and He established this by mentioning the disbelieving wrongdoers, so as to clarify the difference between the two conditions. His saying, ﴿for Us﴾ means: for Our good pleasure and seeking Our reward. As-Suddi and others said: this verse was revealed before the obligation of fighting (al-qital).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It was before the conventional jihad (al-jihad al-'urfi), and it is rather a general jihad in the religion of Allah, the Exalted, and seeking His pleasure. Al-Hasan said: the verse refers to worship (al-'ibad). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibrahim ibn Adham said: it refers to those who act upon what they know. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah will teach him what he does not know." Some scholars drew upon His saying, ﴿And fear Allah; and Allah teaches you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. Some scholars said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him: "Our shortcoming in knowing what we do not know is only caused by our shortcoming in acting upon what we know." Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: "The jihad in this verse is not merely fighting the enemy; rather it is the support of the religion, refuting the falsifiers, suppressing the wrongdoers, and its greatest form is commanding good and forbidding evil." Among it is also striving against the self in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and this is (p-661) the greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar), as said by al-Hasan and others. There is a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ regarding it: "You have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said to Ibn al-Mubarak: "When you see people have differed, then hold fast to the mujahidun and the people of the frontiers, for Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. Indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾" Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of the verse is: "And those who strive in emigration, We will surely guide them to the way of steadfastness upon faith." The word "sabil" here may mean the paths and roads of Paradise, and it may mean the way of deeds that lead to Paradise and the luminous creeds. Yusuf ibn Asbat said: "It is the rectification of intention in deeds, and the love of increase and understanding. This means that the servant is rewarded for his goodness with an increase in goodness, and knows with the newness of what he knows is ahead; and this is the state of one with whom Allah is pleased." The rest of the verse is a promise.

"Ma'a" (مَعَ) may be a noun here, which is why the lam of emphasis entered upon it; and it may be a particle, and the lam entered because of the sense of stability it carries, as in: "Indeed Zayd is surely in the house" (إنَّ زَيْدًا لَفي الدارِ).

The commentary on Surah al-'Ankabut is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

And blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.
